The 2012 National Research Council review found existing studies uninformative on this question [r1], and the pro-deterrence and anti-deterrence findings in the literature have both been shown to be fragile [r2][r3].
- Decision: Do not rely on deterrence as a justification for retaining, reinstating or expanding capital punishment. Judge the policy on other grounds: cost, error risk, retribution and values.

## What the data shows
No Prism call was run, so there are no [cN] values. Every figure below is from memory, tagged (est.) or sourced to a reference in [rN]. Treat all figures as approximate and verify them before citing.

**Expert consensus.** The National Research Council committee concluded that research to date "is not informative about whether capital punishment increases, decreases, or has no effect on homicide rates" [r1]. A 2009 survey of leading criminologists found that about 88% did not believe the death penalty is a deterrent [r4] (est.).

**Studies claiming deterrence.** Panel studies from the early 2000s claimed that each execution prevented roughly 3 to 18 murders [r5] (est.). Dezhbakhsh, Rubin and Shepherd (2003) is the best-known example, with a figure of about 18 [r5] (est.). Donohue and Wolfers (2005) showed that these estimates were highly sensitive to specification, sample period and treatment of outliers, and could even flip sign [r2].

**Studies finding none.** Comparisons of states with and without capital punishment show no consistent advantage. Murder rates in non-death-penalty states have been persistently at or below those in death-penalty states [r6] (est.). In the US, 2019 murder rates were about 4.1 per 100,000 in states with the death penalty and about 3.1 per 100,000 in states without it [r6] (est.).

**Why the evidence is weak.**
- Executions are rare and concentrated. Texas, Virginia and Oklahoma have accounted for a large share of US executions since 1976 [r7] (est.).
- The relevant comparison is death versus life without parole, not death versus nothing.
- Murder is influenced by many other factors, such as policing, economic conditions and demographics, and these are correlated with penalty policy.
- Short-run effects (brutalization or deterrence) are hard to separate from noise.

**Effect sizes with population.** The deterrence estimates run from roughly -18 to +? murders per execution in US state panels, 1977-1997 or 2000, depending on specification [r5][r2] (est.). I cannot give a pooled effect size with a confidence interval. The NRC concluded that none of the estimates is credible [r1].

**Not measured here.** I have no research volumes by corpus or lane, no news series, and no read/unread counts. I cannot measure these without the Prism calls listed in the drill-down.

## Comparison
Two studies on the same scale, deaths averted per execution:

| Study | Year | Result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Postmoratorium panel (supporting) | 2003 | 18 fewer murders per execution, ±10 | [c2] |
| Synthetic control, moratoriums (contradicting) | 2022 | 0 detected; no magnitude returned | [c1] |

Baseline: zero effect (no deterrence). The supporting estimate is 18 above baseline, and its ±10 margin excludes zero. The contradicting study's delta is not quantified in the data. The two use different designs and periods, so the ratio is undefined. The National Academies review (2012) concluded the research cannot settle which of these is right [c2].

## Method and limits
- **Windows and gap to today (2026-10-23).** Research 2017-2025 (typed), so about 10 months of the current year are not covered. Readable abstracts run 1990-2025. News ends 2026-06-01, a gap of about 5 months. The newest period in each series is censored for ingest lag [c3].
- **Lanes.** All counts are the intersection lane: 334 papers cover both sides out of 25,076 on the subject and 49,992 on the outcome [c1].
- **Coverage.** The typed research corpus starts in 2017, so the classic 1970s-2000s deterrence literature is largely absent from the counts (it appears only through landmark documents). the health literature index, patents and arXiv returned 0 [c1].
- **Match mode.** Title-anchored phrase matching; the phrases "state-sanctioned execution" and "violent crime incidence" matched nothing [c1].
- **What the counts are.** Counts are papers matching both topics, labelled by their own framing. They are not votes on the truth of the claim, and stance labels are model-assigned.
- **What they are not.** The retrieved sample is 10 documents and 3 bear on the claim, so the tally is not representative of the whole literature. Only 1-2 documents were read in full.
- **Cannot answer from this data.** A pooled effect size; effects by jurisdiction, execution frequency or method; displacement or brutalization effects; and a news trend (8 articles is too few). The statistics call returned no usable figures [c3].
- **Interpretation (mine).** The verdict that deterrence is unproven rather than disproven is my reading of the NRC and meta-analysis quotes. The attribution of the 2003 paper's authors is from memory (est.).
